Adam Stenavich.blurb: Stenavich's system doesn't have a defining stylistic signature — pass tendency, play-action, screens, and tempo all sit at or near league average, and an exoticness score of 54 puts him squarely in the middle of the pack. What stands out is pre-snap motion at 47% (against a ~41% norm) and a modestly elevated RPO rate, but neither is dramatic. What is dramatic is the output: +0.07 EPA/play, 12th among 82 coaches — though that number is difficult to separate from the Jordan Love era in Green Bay, so treat it as context, not proof of scheme value on its own.

Andy Reid.blurb: Reid's Kansas City offense passes more than almost anyone — sixth-most pass-heavy by tendency — and leans on pre-snap motion (50%, well above the 41% league norm) and screens (10% vs. 7% average) to manufacture leverage before and after the snap. RPO usage is genuinely unusual, sitting at 4% against a 2% league average, one of the highest rates in the sample. Results are strong at +0.06 EPA/play, though the scheme value reads as only middling — and with Mahomes under center, that number can't be fully trusted as a system read on its own.

Ben Johnson.blurb: Ben Johnson's system sits in the elite tier on scheme value (+0.106, third of 82 callers) and it earns that through a few deliberate commitments rather than a broad bag of tricks. Play-action at 26% — well above the 18% league norm — is the clearest signature; he uses it more than almost anyone, and the offense produces at +0.09 EPA/play to back it up. He's slightly run-heavier than average and almost never touches RPOs (1% vs. a 2% norm), so the play-action isn't window dressing on a spread system — it has a genuine run game behind it. Tempo is real too, at 82 plays per game against a 75-play average, and pre-snap motion sits modestly above norm. The creativity score of 60 reflects a system with genuine variety, but Johnson's edge looks more structural than exotic.

Brian Schottenheimer.blurb: Schottenheimer's Dallas offense sits almost exactly at league average across every structural dimension — motion at 44% (norm: 41%), play-action at 20% (norm: 18%), RPO and screen usage both at the median. The one notable lean is tempo, running 81 plays per game against a league norm of 75, which at least reflects a consistent pace preference. Results landed slightly above average at +0.05 EPA/play, but this system ran behind one quarterback throughout, so whether that reflects scheme value or quarterback value genuinely can't be separated.

Drew Petzing.blurb: Drew Petzing runs a genuinely conventional offense — creativity, motion, pass tendency, and tempo all sit within a rounding error of league average. The one real departure is play-action at 22%, a few ticks above the 18% norm, which fits a run-heavy identity without being a defining feature. Scheme value lands at +0.015 against a league average of -0.012, and results are modestly positive at +0.02 EPA/play — a functional system that produces, but doesn't do it through anything exotic.

Jim Bob Cooter.blurb: Cooter's Indianapolis offense ran pretty close to league average across most dimensions — motion, tempo, screens, and overall creativity all land right at the middle of the pack. The standout is play-action usage at 23%, well above the 18% league norm, paired with a modest RPO presence; he clearly preferred to keep defenses honest with pre-snap and post-snap run fakes rather than volume passing, as a below-average pass tendency (-3.1 over expected vs. -0.9 league norm) confirms. Results were essentially neutral at -0.03 EPA/play, which is unremarkable but not damning for a run-leaning system.

Kellen Moore.blurb: Moore's system sits right at league average on nearly every structural dimension — creativity, pass tendency, play-action, screens — with one genuine outlier: pre-snap motion on 50% of dropbacks, well above the 41% norm, which is the clearest fingerprint of his approach. The scheme value of +0.023 against a league average of -0.012 suggests the system itself generates positive expected value above the personnel, though results have landed at middling EPA. Straightforward in design, with execution doing the heavier lifting than schematic complexity.

Kevin O'Connell.blurb: O'Connell's offense is more creative than most — 57th percentile on exoticness, driven by a genuinely high play-action rate at 24% against an 18% league norm — but the results haven't matched the design. Scheme value sits at -0.049 against a league average of -0.012, and EPA/play at -0.06 trails the field too. Most other levers — motion, tempo, RPOs — are right at the middle of the league. The tools are there; the production hasn't been.

Kyle Shanahan.blurb: Shanahan's system ranks first in scheme value among the 82 play-callers in this index, and the results back it up — +0.13 EPA/play, fourth overall. The defining mechanic is pre-snap motion: 60% of dropbacks, against a league norm of 41%, which is what makes an otherwise conventional-looking offense genuinely difficult to defend. Play-action, tempo, and pass tendency all sit right at league average; this isn't an exotic system by design, it just creates leverage through relentless pre-snap manipulation and execution.

Matt LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's system sits near the top of the league in scheme value — +0.116 against a league average of -0.012 — though with Jordan Love running it, that number is indicative rather than definitive. What's notable is how ordinary the stylistic profile is: motion at 47% (league avg 41%), play-action and tempo both right at average, and a mild run lean that's barely outside the norm. The results are genuinely strong (+0.07 EPA/play, #14), but this is a system built on execution and fit, not exotic design.

Matt Nagy.blurb: Nagy runs a pass-heavy system — sitting ninth in PROE at +3.3 over expected, meaningfully above the league norm — and leans on RPOs at roughly double the average rate (4% vs. 2%). Most other levers sit close to the middle: motion at 47% is modestly above the 41% norm, play-action and tempo are ordinary, and the scheme itself scores a 45 on creativity against a 50 average. Scheme value comes in at +0.021 against a league average of -0.012, but with only moderate reliability given the quarterback dependency, treat that as a directional read rather than a firm verdict.

Mike LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's system leans on pre-snap motion — 53% of dropbacks, well above the league's 41% norm — as its clearest structural feature, with play-action also running a few ticks above average at 22%. Everything else sits close to league norms: tempo, screen rate, and pass tendency are all middle of the pack, and the scheme registers as conventionally structured overall. The results were modestly positive at +0.04 EPA/play, but this offense ran through one quarterback, so there's no clean way to separate what the scheme produced from what the QB did.

Mike McDaniel.blurb: McDaniel runs one of the most structurally unusual offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 61% of dropbacks (league average is 41%) puts him in the top three, and he layers in screens at nearly double the league rate. What he doesn't do is throw much: pass rate over expected sits at -5.1, among the lowest in the league. The creativity is real, but the scheme value comes in at -0.055 against a league average of -0.012, which is a number worth taking seriously even if the results land in the middle of the pack.

Sean McVay.blurb: McVay's system has three consistent signatures: pre-snap motion at 54% (well above the 41% league norm), play-action at 23% (versus 18% league average), and almost no RPOs — under 1% against a 2% norm. Everything else, including tempo and screen rate, sits right at league average, and the creativity score of 52 puts him squarely in the middle of the pack. The scheme-value number is indicative rather than precise given the quarterback dependency, but the results — +0.06 EPA/play — are solidly positive.

Sean Payton.blurb: Payton's Denver offense sits close to league average on most surface dimensions — tempo, play-action, motion, and creativity all land right at the norm — but a few things stand out: screens at 10% (league average is 7%) and an RPO rate that's modest but above average at 3%. The bigger story is the scheme value: +0.024 against a league average of -0.012, ranking 13th of 82, suggesting the system is generating real structural advantage beyond what the quarterback and matchups explain. Results bear that out — essentially break-even EPA in what was a transitional roster situation.

Shane Steichen.blurb: Steichen's system sits quietly above the league in actual value — +0.039 against a league average of -0.012, ninth among 82 coaches — without doing anything visually exotic to get there. The clearest fingerprints are a play-action rate of 23% (league average is 18%) and a run-lean tendency that sits modestly below the passing norm, both suggesting a system built around structured, constraint-heavy offense rather than volume throwing. Most other dimensions — motion, tempo, screens, creativity — land right at the league median. The -0.03 EPA/play is a mild negative result, worth watching, but scheme value and raw output don't always move together in the short run.

Todd Monken.blurb: Todd Monken's Cleveland offense scores well on scheme value — +0.045 against a league average of -0.012, good for eighth overall — without doing much that's structurally unusual. Motion, play-action, tempo, screen rate, RPO usage: every dimension sits almost exactly at league norms. What stands out is that a genuinely conventional system is still generating above-average EPA, which suggests the value comes from execution and play design quality rather than any schematic edge.

Wes Phillips.blurb: Phillips ran a conventional-tempo, middle-of-the-pack offense in Minnesota with one meaningful structural signature: play-action on 24% of dropbacks, well above the 18% league norm and top ten among the 82 coaches indexed. Everything else — motion, RPOs, screens, pass tendency — sits right at league average. The results were slightly below average at -0.06 EPA/play, though four seasons across a roster in transition makes it hard to pin that cleanly on the scheme.

Zac Taylor.blurb: Taylor runs one of the more pass-heavy systems in the league — +8.8 over expected pass rate, second among all play-callers — while keeping almost everything else right at the median: motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage are all league-average. The creativity score (39/100, well below the 50 norm) confirms this isn't a system built on disguise or exotic concepts; it's a conventional structure that leans on volume passing to generate value. The scheme grades out at +0.035 above a QB-adjusted baseline, ranking tenth overall, which suggests the system itself carries real worth beyond just the quarterback.

Bobby Slowik.blurb: Slowik's system ranks in the top 10 league-wide on creativity — 57/100 against a 50/100 norm — which makes it one of the more structurally inventive offenses in the league, even if almost nothing else stands out. Pass tendency, play-action, motion, tempo, and screen rate all sit right at the league average. The scheme-value read is indicative at best given the QB entanglement, but the results so far (-0.04 EPA/play, below the -0.01 norm) suggest the creativity hasn't translated into production yet.

Brad Idzik.blurb: Idzik's offense in Carolina is about as close to league-average as a system gets — pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and creativity all sit within a point or two of the norm. The one real deviation is pre-snap motion, which he uses on just 33% of dropbacks against a ~41% league average, making this a comparatively static offense pre-snap. Results land right at the middle of the pack (-0.02 EPA/play), and scheme value reads as a modest positive, though with only moderate reliability given the quarterback dependency, that number is indicative at best, not a clean verdict on the system itself.

Dan Pitcher.blurb: Dan Pitcher ran one of the most pass-heavy systems in the league during his Cincinnati tenure — a +8.9 PROE that ranked first among 82 coordinators, and it wasn't subtle. Everything else sat near league average: motion at 40%, tempo at 76 plays per game, play-action at 14% (a tick below the 18% norm). The results were strong at +0.07 EPA/play, but this system ran almost entirely through one quarterback, so how much of that belongs to the scheme versus the personnel is genuinely hard to separate.

Frank Smith.blurb: Frank Smith's system is defined by pre-snap complexity — motion on 70% of dropbacks (league average is 41%, and nobody in this sample ran it higher) and screens at nearly double the league rate, which together create a structure built around manufacturing easy decisions and controlled touches. Play-action at 25% against an 18% norm adds another layer. Pass tendency runs slightly run-heavy, tempo is ordinary, and the offensive EPA landed middling — so the exoticness of the design didn't translate into a meaningful edge in results.

Joe Brady.blurb: Brady's system sits in genuinely rare territory on creativity — 64/100 against a league average of 50, fourth among 82 play-callers — built heavily on pre-snap motion (52% of dropbacks, well above the ~41% norm) while pass tendency, play-action, and tempo all land right at league average. The results have been elite (+0.17 EPA/play, second overall), though scheme value is only moderate-confidence here because it's difficult to fully untangle the system's worth from the quarterback running it. What's clear is the identity: unusual structural complexity at the line of scrimmage, conventional everywhere else.

Joe Lombardi.blurb: Lombardi's Denver offense leaned on a few tools pretty heavily — play-action at 24% (league average is 18%), screens at 12% (roughly double the league norm), and RPOs at 4% — while keeping everything else close to the middle: ordinary creativity score, ordinary motion, ordinary tempo. The results matched the profile: dead even at +0.00 EPA/play, essentially average. Nothing broken, nothing that jumps off the page either.

Klint Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's system sits in an interesting middle ground: the creativity score (57/100, above the ~50 league average) is driven largely by pre-snap motion, which he deploys on half of all dropbacks against a ~41% norm, while nearly everything else — play-action, tempo, screens, RPOs — runs right at league average. The scheme value is a modest positive (+0.019 vs. a league average of -0.012), and the results land around even, which for a young play-caller in Las Vegas reads as quietly functional rather than inspiring. The one honest flag: he runs slightly more conservative pass tendencies than expected, which may reflect personnel constraints more than philosophy.

Liam Coen.blurb: Liam Coen's scheme reads almost deliberately conventional on the surface — motion, tempo, play-action, and RPO usage all sit right at league average, and his creativity score of 51 is about as middle-of-the-pack as it gets. What separates him is the output: +0.101 scheme value ranks fourth among 82 play-callers, and the offense is producing +0.11 EPA/play, sixth in that same pool. The case Coen makes is that execution and design quality don't require exoticism to beat the league.

Nathaniel Hackett.blurb: Hackett's system in Arizona was about as vanilla as it gets — pre-snap motion at 30% against a 41% league norm, a creativity score of 37 out of 100 (73rd of 82 coordinators), and virtually every other dial sitting right at the median. The results were poor, -0.10 EPA/play against a -0.01 league average, though how much of that belongs to the scheme versus the roster is a fair question. What's clear is that nothing in the design was built to create structural advantages.

Press Taylor.blurb: Press Taylor's system is about as close to league-average as it gets — pass tendency, play-action, motion, RPO, and tempo all sit right at the norm, and the results land exactly at the league median too. The one signal worth noting is a +0.033 scheme value, which ranks 11th and suggests the system generated real efficiency above what the opponent and quarterback adjustments account for — though with moderate reliability, that number is indicative rather than definitive, and Chicago cycled through enough QB situations that clean separation is hard. A conventional scheme that may have quietly done more with less.

Zac Robinson.blurb: Robinson's system sits close to league average on nearly every structural dimension — tempo, screens, RPOs, play-action all within a few ticks of normal. The clearest deviation is run-heaviness: his offenses pass 8 percentage points less than expected given game context, the third-lowest rate in the sample. Pre-snap motion at 48% runs modestly above the 41% norm, but that's the lone wrinkle in an otherwise conventional framework, and the scheme value of -0.069 against a league average of -0.012 suggests the system hasn't generated much of an edge yet.

Alex Van Pelt.blurb: Van Pelt ran the fastest-paced offense in the sample by a significant margin — 86 plays per game against a league average of 75 — but pace alone didn't produce results: -0.11 EPA/play ranked 68th of 82. Everything else sits near league average: screens ran slightly above norm at 9%, motion and play-action were ordinary, and the overall scheme creativity score came in below average at 42. The structure is conventional, the tempo is aggressive, and the outcomes were poor.

Arthur Smith.blurb: Arthur Smith runs a run-leaning offense — his pass rate sits 3.5 points below expectation against a league average of just -0.9 — built around two genuine tendencies: play-action at 23% (league average 18%) and screens at 10% (league average 7%). Those aren't decorative; they're the architecture of a system that creates leverage off the run. Everything else — motion, tempo, RPOs — is basically league average, and the results land right there too, at -0.01 EPA/play. Solidly middle of the pack, which tracks for a scheme that's more about constraint football than invention.

Declan Doyle.blurb: Doyle's system lands in the top six on scheme value and the top five in creativity, though both numbers carry an asterisk — with only moderate separation from the quarterback, they're directionally useful but not definitive. What's actually distinctive is the exotic element: a creativity score of 61 against a league average of 50 suggests real structural variety in how he designs plays, even as motion, tempo, play-action, and pass tendency all sit squarely at league norm. The results (+0.05 EPA/play, nineteenth overall) are solid without needing a gimmick to explain them.

Doug Nussmeier.blurb: Nussmeier's two seasons in New Orleans produced an offense that sits near the middle of the pack on almost every structural dimension — pass rate, tempo, motion, RPO usage all within a few ticks of league average. The one real departure is screens, which he ran at 4% against a 7% norm, suggesting a deliberate choice to avoid short-yardage releases. Results landed at -0.06 EPA/play, modestly below average, though how much of that reflects scheme versus roster is the honest question here.

Eric Bieniemy.blurb: Bieniemy's Kansas City offense was notably pass-heavy — +7.2 over expected pass rate, fourth among 82 coordinators — while keeping most other dials close to league average: motion at 31% (below the 41% norm), play-action at 15% (below 18%), and a relaxed tempo of 71 plays per game. The results were fine but unspectacular at +0.01 EPA/play. What the numbers genuinely can't answer is how much of any of this was Bieniemy and how much was Patrick Mahomes — that separation simply isn't possible from one quarterback over two seasons, and that's the honest read on what this entry tells you.

Grant Udinski.blurb: Udinski's Jacksonville offense doesn't stand out stylistically — motion, play-action, screens, and tempo all sit right at or just below league average, and the scheme rates middle of the pack on overall creativity. What stands out is the output: +0.10 EPA/play, seventh-best among 82 coordinators in the sample. That's a results-over-style profile, and it's worth noting he no longer calls the plays in Jacksonville.

Greg Roman.blurb: Roman's system in Los Angeles is built around two things that genuinely stand out: play-action at 27% of dropbacks (league average is 18%, good for second in the league) and pre-snap motion on 52% of snaps, well above the 41% norm. Everything else — creativity, tempo, RPO usage, screens — lands right around average. The indicative scheme value of +0.032 is encouraging, but given the sample and quarterback dependency, it's honest to hold that loosely; results so far are middling at +0.01 EPA/play.

Josh McDaniels.blurb: McDaniels ran one of the more conventional systems in the league during this window — motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all sitting right at or just below average — but the results were strong, finishing fifth in EPA/play at +0.11 against a league average of -0.01. The honest caveat is that the scheme ran with effectively one quarterback, so there's no clean way to separate what the system produced from what the QB produced. The one real stylistic outlier is screens, used at just 4% against a 7% league norm, suggesting a preference for structure over release-valve throws.

Ken Dorsey.blurb: Dorsey's clearest fingerprint is tempo — 85 plays per game ranks second in the league against an average of 75, so Cleveland is genuinely pushing pace in a way most teams don't. The passing lean is real too, running about 2.5 percentage points over expectation (13th), but everything else — motion, play-action, RPOs, screens — sits right at the league median. The problem is the results: -0.04 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, and a scheme value of -0.091 versus the -0.012 norm, meaning the system itself isn't generating much after accounting for personnel.

Klay Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's San Francisco offense ran fewer RPOs than almost anyone (effectively zero, against a 2% league norm) and leaned on pre-snap motion at a well-above-average 52% of dropbacks to manufacture the advantages other systems get through trickery. Pass tendency ran slightly above league norm, play-action and tempo were ordinary, and the results were elite — +0.13 EPA/play, third of 82 — though the honest caveat is that separating scheme from quarterback in that environment is genuinely difficult.

Klayton Adams.blurb: Adams ran one of the more conventional offensive schemes in the league during his time calling plays in Dallas — every structural lever sits right at league average, from motion (41%) to play-action (19%) to tempo. The one real deviation is screens, which he used at 4% against a 7% league norm, suggesting a preference for pushing the ball down the field rather than manufacturing easy touches at the line. What stands out is the results: +0.09 EPA/play, 8th of 82, well above the league average of -0.01 — a reminder that execution within a vanilla structure can still produce elite offense.

Kliff Kingsbury.blurb: Kingsbury's Washington offense is built around two things that genuinely separate it from the league: play-action on 26% of dropbacks (league average is 18%, top-3 in the data set) and RPOs at 4% (double the league norm, also top-3). The result is a pre-snap threat menu that forces defenses to respect the run even when passing, and the offense produced +0.07 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01. The scheme-value number (+0.045, indicative but not precise given the quarterback dependency) suggests the system itself is contributing, though how much belongs to the scheme versus the QB isn't fully separable yet. Motion and pass tendency sit closer to league average, so the identity here isn't complexity for its own sake — it's a specific structural commitment to deception at the line.

Luke Getsy.blurb: Getsy runs a genuinely fast offense — 83 plays per game ranks 8th among the 82 coordinators in this index, well above the 75-play league average — and pairs that tempo with pre-snap motion on 51% of dropbacks, also meaningfully above the 41% norm. Everything else sits at league average: creativity, pass tendency, play-action, RPOs, screens. The problem is the results: -0.10 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, and a scheme value of -0.057 versus the -0.012 norm, both pointing to a system that isn't generating much value for what it's asking offenses to do.

Mike Kafka.blurb: Kafka's Giants ran fast — 83 plays per game puts him in the top tier for tempo — but speed without production is just burning clock efficiently. Nearly everything else sits at league average: motion at 41%, play-action at 21%, RPO and screen usage both unremarkable. The results were genuinely bad, -0.14 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, and the QB-adjusted scheme value lands slightly below average too, which means the personnel context doesn't fully excuse it.

Mike McCarthy.blurb: McCarthy's Pittsburgh offense runs almost entirely down the middle of the league in structure — tempo, motion, play-action, creativity all sit at or near the norm — with one real deviation: he passes more than expected (+2.7 PROE, where the league average is actually below zero). The results haven't justified it, coming in at -0.07 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, and the QB-adjusted scheme value of -0.071 versus the -0.012 norm suggests the system itself isn't adding much either.

Nick Caley.blurb: Nick Caley's Houston offense is almost perfectly average across the board — pass tendency, motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all sit right at or within a rounding error of league norms. The one genuine deviation is screens, where he runs them at 4% against a 7% league average, one of the lower rates in the league. Scheme value comes in slightly below average, though with only moderate reliability it's indicative at best. The results land just above league average EPA/play, which is a reasonable outcome for a system this straightforward.

Nick Holz.blurb: Holz runs a conventional system — creativity, motion, play-action, and tempo all sit near league average — and the one real stylistic signature is a strong lean toward the run, passing about 6.5 percentage points less than expected, which ranks 69th. The results haven't justified the approach: Tennessee's offense sits at -0.14 EPA/play, well below the league average of -0.01. The scheme value lands in the middle of the pack, but at -0.119 against a league average of -0.012, "middle" is being generous.

Shane Waldron.blurb: Shane Waldron's system is largely conventional — creativity, motion, play-action, and pass tendency all sit near league average — with one genuine outlier: screens on 12% of dropbacks, well above the 7% league norm and a top-4 rate league-wide. That's a real structural choice, not noise. The results have been below average at -0.03 EPA/play, and the scheme value ranks 27th, so the screen-heavy approach hasn't translated into offensive efficiency in Chicago.

Tim Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Giants offense runs at a notably high tempo (82 plays per game against a 75-play norm) and leans heavily on play-action (24% vs. 18% league average) and screens (10% vs. 7%), suggesting a system built around rhythm and manufactured easy looks rather than raw creativity — exoticness sits below average at 46/100. The run-heaviness is real: pass rate over expected is -4.3, well below the -0.9 norm. Scheme value lands right at league average, and results do too, which is about what the profile suggests.

Tommy Rees.blurb: Rees runs a decidedly run-heavy system — passing 7.1 percentage points below expectation, which ranks 72nd of 82 coordinators — with pre-snap motion (34%) and RPOs (1%) both sitting below league norms of 41% and 2% respectively. The scheme itself is conventional across most dimensions, and the results have been poor: -0.14 EPA/play ranks 73rd, well below the league average of -0.01. Scheme value comes in at -0.182 against a league average of -0.012, suggesting the system isn't adding much on top of the personnel.

Andrew Janocko.blurb: Janocko's Raiders offense was slower and leaner than almost anyone in the league — 63 plays per game against a 75-play norm, essentially no RPOs, and play-action at 11% when the average sits at 18%. What's notable is that despite stripping out most of the pre-snap complexity — motion at 29% versus a 41% league average, screens nearly absent — the creativity score still lands at 57, suggesting the variety came from structure rather than volume. The results were marginally positive at +0.02 EPA/play, which given the deliberate, low-usage style is a reasonable return.

Brian Angelichio.blurb: Angelichio's Pittsburgh offense was built around throwing the ball more than almost any system in the league — +3.6 over expected pass rate, seventh-highest — but it got there through a stripped-down approach: pre-snap motion at 21% and play-action at 8% were both well below the ~41% and ~18% league norms. No manufactured looks, no tempo pressure at 62 plays per game against a 75-play average. The results landed near neutral at -0.03 EPA/play, which is functional but not an endorsement of the method.

Brian Daboll.blurb: Daboll runs one of the more stripped-down offenses in the league — low motion (21% vs. a ~41% norm), minimal play-action (10% vs. 18%), few screens, and a slow tempo that ranks near the bottom of the sample. It's a deliberately sparse approach, not a creative one, though that's a description rather than a verdict. The catch is that this scheme ran with one quarterback, so what the system actually produces on its own merits can't be cleanly separated from the player running it — the -0.09 EPA/play sits below average, but how much of that is scheme is genuinely unclear.

Brian Fleury.blurb: Fleury runs one of the more deliberate offenses in the league — 63 plays per game against a 75-play norm, almost no play-action (11% vs. 18% average), minimal pre-snap motion (25% vs. 41%), and effectively zero RPOs. The creativity score of 58 sits ninth in the league, which is the real tension here: the concepts are varied, but the pace and structure are stripped down. Results land near the middle at -0.04 EPA/play, though with one quarterback driving the window, what belongs to Fleury and what belongs to the QB genuinely can't be separated.

Chip Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Las Vegas offense in 2023 stands out for two things: pre-snap motion on 56% of dropbacks and play-action on 25% of snaps, both well above league norms of 41% and 18% respectively. Everything else — tempo, RPOs, screens, pass tendency — sits right at league average. The results were poor (-0.21 EPA/play, near the bottom of the league), though with scheme value only moderately separable from the quarterback situation, how much of that is Kelly's system versus personnel is genuinely hard to untangle.

Dave Canales.blurb: Canales runs a conventional scheme by most measures — motion, screens, pass tendency, and play-action all sit near league norms — with two genuine outliers: tempo (81 plays per game, well above the 75-play average) and RPO usage (4%, double the league rate and sixth-highest in the sample). The results landed at essentially league-average EPA/play, but because this offense ran through one quarterback, the system's actual worth can't be separated from that quarterback's contribution.

David Blough.blurb: Blough's Washington offense is defined as much by what it strips out as what it runs — play-action at 10% (league norm is 18%), pre-snap motion at 25% (norm is 41%), screens near zero, RPOs effectively nonexistent, and a tempo of 62 plays per game against a league average of 75. It's a deliberately sparse system, and the results land right at league average (-0.01 EPA/play), though scheme value is only moderately separable from the quarterback's contribution. Call it functional minimalism: the approach works well enough, but it's hard to know yet how much of that is the system.

Davis Webb.blurb: Webb's one season calling plays in Denver was about as stripped-down as it gets: pre-snap motion at 24% and play-action at 10% were both well below league norms of 41% and 18%, and the offense ran at a notably slow pace (56 plays per game against a league average of 75). The results landed right around average at -0.02 EPA/play, which is something, given how little the scheme asked of the pre-snap game.

Frank Reich.blurb: Reich's Jets offense was about as stripped-down as it gets — pre-snap motion at 18% (league average is 41%), play-action at 9% (versus 18%), and one of the slowest tempos in the sample at 58 plays per game. The system was conventional almost across the board, which makes the +0.04 EPA/play finish respectable on its face, but this ran almost entirely through one quarterback, so there's no clean way to separate what the scheme contributed from what the QB did.

John Morton.blurb: Morton's Detroit offense ran leaner on passing than almost any system in the league — 5.1 percentage points below expected pass rate, against a league norm of just -0.9 — but compensated with structural advantages at the line of scrimmage: pre-snap motion on 59% of dropbacks (league norm 41%) and play-action at 26% (league norm 18%) are both top-five rates.
